posts.text:
This is basic accounting. When you have a bank deposit you hold an asset and the bank has a liability. Reserves are an asset for the bank and a liability of the Fed. But the Fed's liability is to the bank, not to you. You don't have a claim on reserves because they aren't your asset and they aren't the bank's liability to you. Your claim is on the bank, full stop.

You can't even hold reserves. Only banks and a handful of other institutions with Fed accounts can. When you send money to someone at another bank, your bank settles with their bank in reserves. Your deposit goes away and they get a new one, but the reserves never touch your hands.

The one time you end up holding a Fed liability is when you withdraw cash. Your bank swaps reserves for paper currency and hands it to you. That's a Fed liability, but it's a different one. It isn't reserves.

posts.text:
The dollar’s continued strength despite the technology selloff is particularly revealing. Deutsche Bank data show aggressive overseas buying of U.S. equity ETFs during the decline. These foreign investors include international pension funds, sovereign wealth funds, insurance companies, and other institutions based outside the United States.

Much of this buying reflects America’s dominance in global equity benchmarks, expectations that U.S. corporations will continue capturing a disproportionate share of global profits, and institutional portfolio rebalancing during market corrections. Dollar appreciation can also benefit unhedged foreign investors, while elevated American interest rates and global rate differentials continue supporting the currency.

But these inflows may be temporarily cushioning U.S. equities even as underlying financial conditions deteriorate. Importantly, foreign ETF inflows do not necessarily represent entirely new dollar demand, since investors may already hold dollars or hedge their currency exposure. The broader concern is how dependent American financial markets have become on sustained international capital flows, particularly with valuations heavily concentrated in technology and AI.

If foreign investors begin withdrawing capital while the Fed continues tightening, equities could lose an important source of support precisely when dollar financing becomes more expensive for overseas borrowers. That could accelerate global deleveraging and intensify selling across financial markets. Dollar strength alone doesn’t establish a liquidity crisis, but if foreign inflows reverse while the dollar continues appreciating and offshore funding costs rise, it would become a much more serious warning of an emerging global dollar squeeze.

quoted.text: "Why is the dollar rallying even as US tech stocks have sold off so much?" asks Deutsche Bank's George Saravelos, who expected the opposite would happen. His explanation: rate differentials and the fact that foreigners have been big buyers of the US equity dip, at least for now
